title: Blombos Cave ochre engravings
summary: Excavators at Blombos Cave in South Africa recovered pieces of red ochre engraved with abstract patterns in Middle Stone Age layers. Thermoluminescence dating of burnt stone gave a mean age of 77,000 years for the layers, and the Smithsonian lists the plaque as 77,000 to 75,000 years old. The authors argue the finds show modern human behavior in Africa long before the Upper Paleolithic.

uncertainty.note: Converted as year = 1950 minus age. Start is the 77,000-year mean date of the engraved-ochre layers (thermoluminescence); end is the 75,000 lower figure on the Smithsonian page. An overlying dune gave 70,000 years (OSL) as a younger limit.

as_recorded.value: A mean date of 77,000 years was obtained for the layers containing the engraved ochres

where.modern_name: Blombos Cave, Western Cape, South Africa
where.historical_name: Blombos Cave, southern Cape coast; no polities exist at this date

importance.justification: Engraved abstract designs cited as evidence for symbolic behavior by early Homo sapiens in Africa.

reviewer_note: Pin is the Wikidata point for the cave; the abstract and Smithsonian page give no coordinates. Dates differ slightly (77,000 mean for the layers; 77,000-75,000 for the plaque); later engravings from the cave are not covered. The Smithsonian says some researchers read the marks as information rather than decoration, so the symbolic reading is an interpretation (confidence probable).
